description: The Community Action Plan for Seismic Safety, or CAPSS, was a nine-year, $1 million study begun in 1998 in San Francisco's Department of Building Inspection to understand and reduce the city's earthquake risk. The Applied Technology Council studied four probable earthquakes and found they would damage many thousands of buildings beyond occupancy, devastate the housing stock, displace middle- and low-income residents for years, kill hundreds of people and cost billions of dollars, borne mostly by owners who lack earthquake insurance. A community advisory committee met more than thirty times over two and a half years and produced 17 recommendations, among them evaluating and retrofitting wood-frame residential buildings of three or more storeys and five or more units, evaluating all buildings, incentives, a retrofit database, a facade ordinance and gas shut-off valves. In December 2010 the mayor formed the Earthquake Safety Implementation Committee, which set up a 30-year work plan in late 2011. The city's page lists the ATC 52-1 to 52-4 reports, including soft-story building safety and post-earthquake repair. Access: free web page and reports. Caveats: the page states goals and recommendations, not measured outcomes of retrofits. It relates to the catalogued soft-story retrofit case study, and gives building loss scenarios for hazard exposure.
